messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Rabbi
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared, Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rabbi Ezra Mandel is a 63-year-old man who has served the same Conservative congregation in a mid-sized Midwestern city for nearly two decades. He came to the United States as a young man, having fled political violence in his country of origin during a period of brutal civil unrest, and he built his life here with deliberate intention — his faith, his community, his role as a spiritual guide all constructed as a kind of answer to what he had survived. He has been in a long-term relationship for eleven years. He has not, until now, sought professional help for what happened to him forty years ago.

Ezra was nineteen when soldiers came to the refugee camp where his family had been sheltering for several months. The raid happened at night. There was shouting — not the ordinary raised voices of argument but the particular quality of shouting that carries absolute authority over life, the kind that means compliance or death. Men with rifles moved through the rows of makeshift shelters, pulling people by the arms and shoulders, and Ezra was grabbed from behind without warning, his body yanked backward before he had registered that anyone was near him. He was held at gunpoint for what he estimates was several hours while others around him were beaten and, in at least two cases, killed. He was eventually released. He crossed into a neighboring country on foot and eventually made his way to the United States through a resettlement program. He has spoken of this history publicly, in sermons, in interfaith panels, in Holocaust remembrance contexts — always in the third person of history, never in the first person of his own nervous system.

What he did not speak about, and what has been accumulating quietly for decades, is the way his body refused to accept that the camp was finished. When a congregant places a hand on his shoulder during a moment of pastoral comfort — a gesture he himself enacts with others dozens of times a week — something seizes in his chest and his hands go cold. He has learned to manage this with a kind of practiced stillness, but he is aware, and he hates that he is aware, that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is standing in his own sanctuary. During services, he has for years selected his position at the bimah not only for liturgical reasons but because from that spot he can see both exits. When he attends community events outside the synagogue, he arrives early and locates the seat nearest a wall. There are perhaps three or four locations in his city where he feels something close to ease.

The shouting is the most intrusive trigger in his daily life. When voices are raised — a domestic dispute audible through an open window, a parent scolding a child in a parking lot, even the televised argument of a political debate — his concentration dissolves entirely. He finds himself unable to follow a line of Talmudic commentary, unable to complete a sentence he is writing. His congregants have noticed, though they have not named it, that his sermons sometimes lose their thread.

Over the months preceding his referral, Ezra has grown quieter with his partner. Not cold, but at a remove — available in practical ways, present at meals, but resistant to the kind of sustained emotional closeness that his partner has gently named as missing. Ezra tells himself he is protecting his partner from something he cannot fully articulate. He has also, in his private moments, been visited by a thought he finds deeply shameful and that he has not shared with anyone: that someone else — someone braver, someone more alert — would have found a way to stop what happened that night. That he failed, somehow, in a way that is both unspecified and total. He tells himself he deserves to carry this. He fills the hours he might spend in reflection with administrative work, correspondence, the endless logistics of congregational life.

What finally brought him to seek help was a bar mitzvah last spring. A family friend, in celebration, fired a party popper behind him. The sound and the sudden touch of confetti on the back of his neck sent him to his knees in front of two hundred people. He has not been able to fully account for himself since. He comes to therapy hoping, he says carefully, to be useful again. What he is most afraid of is that he cannot be trusted — not by others, and not by himself.
